newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's tax crackdown working --Interior Minister.
newsitem.headline: Russia's tax crackdown working --Interior Minister.

text.p: Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Thursday that Russia's crackdown on corporate tax dodging was starting to yield results, raking badly-needed cash into the state coffers.

Kulikov, one of the few conservative ministers left in the upper echelons of President Boris Yeltsin's new reformist government, also lashed back at critics who accuse him of undermining peace efforts in breakaway Chechnya.
"We can say today with certainty that closer cooperation between different government departments is bringing positive results," Kulikov told a news conference.

He said that in the past three months some 600,000 firms guilty of tax avoidance had been exposed and more than half of them investigated. As a result billions of roubles had been paid back to the federal budget, Kulikov added.

Government ministers regularly blame rampant tax dodging by both firms and individuals for recurring shortfalls in state revenues that in turn leads to long delays in payment of pensions and wages to millions of Russians.
Yeltsin's revamped government, led by pro-market liberals, has made the clampdown on tax evasion a key part of its strategy to revive Russia's stagnant economy.
Kulikov said the authorities had found some 100 companies had cheated the tax authorities by setting up surrogate firms that owed the state budget more than seven trillion roubles.
He said a similar crackdown on illegal alcohol production had raked in fines totalling 2.3 billion roubles.
In the northern Caucasus region alone some 200 enterprises illegally producing alcohol had been uncovered, Kulikov added.

Kulikov, a four-star general who appeared on Thursday in his habitual khaki army uniform decorated with medal ribbons, generally takes a severe line on the northern Caucasus, scene of Russia's military debacle in the 21-month long Chechen conflict.
Asked about claims that he was reluctant to help peace efforts there, Kulikov said he was ready to cooperate with the Chechen authorities but said they remained distrustful of him and his ministry.
Kulikov was a robust supporter of Moscow's ill-fated military bid to crush Chechnya's drive for independence.
Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov accused Kulikov on Tuesday of trying to derail the peace process in Chechnya.
"When everything's fine in Chechnya and everything's fine between Russia and Chechnya, then it's bad for Kulikov," Maskhadov said.

Kulikov disagreed. "There are (criminal) bands and groups which are under the control of nobody, not even of (Chechen President Aslan) Maskhadov. We are ready to offer help but we encounter a great distrust (from the Chechen side)...Maskhadov does not trust Kulikov."

Kulikov's ministry has also been fighting an explosion in organised crime across the vast Russian Federation. He recently acknowledged that his cash-strapped security forces had difficulty finding the resources to tackle the criminals.

He said post-communist Russia's soaring crime rate had exacerbated the country's already serious prison overcrowding and had persuaded him to back calls for an amnesty for some categories of criminal.
"Unfortunately this is inevitable. We have to attentively examine this option," he said.
Interfax news agency quoted Russia's general prosecutor recently as saying that he was considering offering an amnesty to some 400,000 prisoners.
Kulikov said the amnesty, if approved, was unlikely to happen before the end of this year.
